subject: economics
title: Cambridge IGCSE Economics (0455)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge IGCSE Economics 0455 syllabus for 2027, 2028 and 2029 (version 1)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings and their numbers (1 to 6, 1.1 to 6.4) are transcribed from the subject content of the official syllabus; objective codes are the syllabus's own content numbers (for example 2.6.2), and where we split or merged content numbers into one node the node code says so (for example 2.2.2-2.2.3; 2.10.3a to 2.10.3c are ours, splitting 2.10.3). Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase; no syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Read 2026-10-08 from the official PDF (version 1, for exams in 2027, 2028 and 2029): the six topics, every numbered subtopic and content item, the assessment overview, the details of the assessment and the list of changes.

This version is examined from 2027. A student sitting the examination in 2026 is examined on the 2023-2025/2026 syllabus, which is not in the repository; the 2027-2029 version is published as the current version because new students now will sit 2027 or later. Changes listed for 2027: Paper 1 increased from 30 to 40 questions and from 45 minutes to 1 hour; Paper 2 reduced from 90 to 80 marks and from 2 hours 15 minutes to 2 hours, with a smaller Question 1; AO3 Evaluation weighting reduced.

Assessment overview as read: all candidates take Paper 1 Multiple Choice (1 hour, 40 marks, 30%, 40 questions on all the content, may include calculations and diagram analysis) and Paper 2 Structured Questions (2 hours, 80 marks, 70%): Section A, one compulsory 20-mark question with parts (a) to (f) based on unseen information about a real economic situation (text, data, possibly tables and diagrams); Section B, three of four 20-mark questions, each introduced by a short context paragraph and with four parts (a) to (d), where part (d) is a two-sided evaluative discussion marked with levels of response. Calculators allowed in both papers. Grades A* to G; no tiers. AO weightings: AO1 43%, AO2 47%, AO3 10% overall (Paper 1: 50/50/0; Paper 2: 40/45/15).

Notes printed in the content: demand and supply diagrams for market failure are not required (2.9); diagrams and perfect or imperfect competition theory are not required for competitive markets and monopoly (3.7). Removed for 2027 (not taught for Cambridge): fixed exchange rate systems, population pyramid interpretation, the claimant count, principles of taxation, deflation content beyond its definition, and PPCs in the context of recession and growth causes.

Not in this syllabus (taught in the family for ZIMSEC only): the three economic systems compared (econ.systems.types), positive and normative statements, PPC shapes (concave, convex and straight-line) beyond shifts, income and cross elasticity, climate change and production as a topic, land reform, location of industry, marginal cost and revenue and profit maximisation, monopolistic competition and market-structure equilibrium, forms of business organisation and sources of finance, SMEs and business plans, national income measurement and its uses and limitations, HIV and AIDS, labour force composition, domestic trade, terms of trade, economic integration, foreign currency shortages, job creation in Zimbabwe and sustainable resource management initiatives.
overview: Cambridge IGCSE Economics covers six topics: the basic economic problem (scarcity, factors of production, opportunity cost, PPCs); the allocation of resources (markets, demand and supply, price determination, elasticity, market and mixed economies, market failure and government intervention); microeconomic decision-makers (money and banking, households, workers, firms, costs and revenue, competitive and monopoly markets); government and the macroeconomy (aims, fiscal, monetary and supply-side policy, growth, unemployment, inflation); economic development (living standards, poverty, population); and international trade and globalisation (specialisation, free trade and restrictions, exchange rates, the current account).
assessmentOverview: All candidates take Paper 1 Multiple Choice (1 hour, 40 questions, 40 marks, 30%) and Paper 2 Structured Questions (2 hours, 80 marks, 70%: one compulsory 20-mark data question in Section A and three of four 20-mark questions in Section B). Calculators may be used in both.

components.name: Paper 1: Multiple Choice
components.description: 40 compulsory multiple-choice questions on all the subject content; may require calculations and the analysis of diagrams.

components.name: Paper 2: Structured Questions
components.description: Section A: one compulsory 20-mark question, parts (a) to (f), on unseen information about a real economic situation. Section B: three of four 20-mark questions, each with parts (a) to (d); part (d) is an evaluative discussion marked by levels.

children.name: The nature of the basic economic problem

objectives.text: Define the basic economic problem and scarcity, with examples for consumers, workers, firms and governments.
Explain the three questions of what, how and for whom to produce.
Distinguish economic goods from free goods.
Define land, labour, capital and enterprise and their rewards.
Explain the causes of changes in the quantity and quality of the factors of production.
Define opportunity cost and give examples in different contexts.
Explain how opportunity cost influences the decisions of consumers, workers, firms and governments.
Define a PPC and draw and interpret a PPC diagram.
Explain the significance of points under, on and beyond a PPC.
Explain movements along a PPC and the opportunity cost they show.
Explain the causes and consequences of shifts of a PPC in terms of economic growth.

children.name: The role of markets in allocating resources

objectives.text: Define a market, give examples and describe the roles of buyers and sellers.
Define demand, link individual and market demand, and draw and interpret a demand diagram.

children.name: Movements along and shifts of a demand curve

objectives.text: Explain the causes of extensions and contractions in demand and illustrate them.
Explain the causes of increases and decreases in demand and illustrate shifts of the demand curve.
Define supply, link individual and market supply, and draw and interpret a supply diagram.

children.name: Movements along and shifts of a supply curve

objectives.text: Explain the causes of extensions and contractions in supply and illustrate them.
Explain the causes of increases and decreases in supply and illustrate shifts of the supply curve.
Explain how the price mechanism answers what, how and for whom to produce.
Define market equilibrium and interpret it from schedules and from demand and supply curves.
Define disequilibrium and interpret shortages and surpluses from schedules and diagrams.
Explain how changes in demand and supply cause price changes.
Explain the effect of price changes on sales and use demand and supply diagrams to show changes in market conditions.
Define price elasticity of demand.
Calculate PED with the formula, interpret its value from perfectly inelastic to perfectly elastic, and draw demand curves showing different PED.
Explain the main influences on whether demand is elastic or inelastic.
Show by diagram and calculation how price changes affect consumer spending and firms' revenue, depending on PED.
Explain the implications of PED for decisions by consumers, workers, firms and government.
Define price elasticity of supply.
Calculate PES with the formula, interpret its value and draw supply curves showing different PES.
Explain the main influences on whether supply is elastic or inelastic.
Define the market economic system.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the market economic system.
Define market failure.
Define public, merit and demerit goods, private, external and social costs and benefits, and monopoly.
Explain the causes of market failure.
Explain the consequences of market failure: over- and under-consumption, non-provision of public goods and monopoly restricting supply (no diagrams).
Define the mixed economic system.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of the mixed economic system.
Define maximum and minimum prices in product markets, draw and interpret their diagrams and explain their advantages and disadvantages.
Define indirect taxes and subsidies, draw and interpret their diagrams and explain their advantages and disadvantages in addressing market failure.

children.name: Regulation, privatisation, nationalisation, direct provision and quotas

objectives.text: Define regulation, privatisation, nationalisation, direct provision and quotas and explain their advantages and disadvantages.
Describe the forms, functions and characteristics of money.
Explain the role and importance of central banks and commercial banks.
Explain how income, the rate of interest, confidence, age and culture influence households' spending, saving and borrowing.
Explain the wage and non-wage factors affecting an individual's choice of occupation.
Explain how labour demand and supply, trade union bargaining power and government policy (including a national minimum wage) determine wages, with diagrams.
Explain why wages differ by skill, sector, sex and between the private and public sectors.
Explain the causes and consequences of changes in the occupational and geographical mobility of labour.
Define division of labour and explain its advantages and disadvantages.
Classify firms as primary, secondary or tertiary and private or public sector, and explain the advantages and disadvantages of small and large firms.
Define horizontal, vertical and conglomerate mergers and explain their advantages and disadvantages with examples.
Explain internal and external economies and diseconomies of scale and draw and interpret average total cost diagrams to show them.

children.name: Demand for factors; labour-intensive and capital-intensive production

objectives.text: Explain the influences on the demand for factors of production.
Explain why firms adopt labour-intensive or capital-intensive production and the advantages and disadvantages of each.
Distinguish production from productivity and explain the influences on them, including changes in investment.
Define total, average total, fixed, average fixed, variable and average variable cost.
Calculate these costs and draw and interpret diagrams of how output affects costs.
Define total revenue and average revenue.
Calculate total and average revenue and explain how sales influence revenue.
Explain survival, social welfare, profit maximisation and growth as objectives of firms.
Explain the characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of competitive markets and the effect of many firms on price, quality, choice and profit (no diagrams).
Explain the characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of monopoly and the effect of one firm on price, quality, choice and profit (no diagrams).
Explain the macroeconomic aims of government, the reasons for and targets of each, and the possible conflicts between them.

children.name: Government budget and spending; fiscal policy measures

objectives.text: Define the government budget, a budget deficit and a budget surplus and calculate their size.
Explain the main areas of government spending and the reasons for and effects of spending in them.
Define fiscal policy.
Describe fiscal policy measures: changes in taxes and government spending.
Explain how fiscal policy may help a government achieve its macroeconomic aims.
Explain the reasons for taxation, classify taxes as progressive, regressive or proportional and direct or indirect, and explain their impact.
Define the money supply and monetary policy.
Describe monetary policy measures: changes in the interest rate, the money supply and the foreign exchange rate.
Explain how monetary policy may help a government achieve its macroeconomic aims.
Define supply-side policy.
Describe supply-side policy measures.
Explain how supply-side policy may help a government achieve its macroeconomic aims.

children.name: Definition, measurement, causes and consequences of growth

objectives.text: Define economic growth.
Explain the measurement of economic growth by real GDP.
Explain the causes of economic growth and its advantages and disadvantages.

children.name: Recession and policies to promote growth

objectives.text: Define recession and explain its causes and consequences.
Evaluate the policies available to promote economic growth.
Define employment, unemployment and full employment.
Explain how unemployment is measured by a labour force survey and calculate the unemployment rate.
Explain frictional, structural, cyclical and seasonal unemployment.

children.name: Consequences of unemployment and policies to reduce it

objectives.text: Explain the consequences of unemployment for individuals, firms, the government and the economy.
Evaluate the policies available to reduce unemployment.

children.name: Inflation, deflation and the causes of inflation

objectives.text: Define inflation and deflation.
Explain demand-pull and cost-push inflation.
Explain how inflation is measured with the Consumer Prices Index.

children.name: Consequences of inflation and policies to control it

objectives.text: Explain how inflation affects savers, lenders, borrowers, consumers, workers, firms and the economy.
Evaluate the policies available to control inflation.
Explain real GDP per head and the Human Development Index as indicators of living standards, with their advantages and disadvantages.

children.name: Comparing living standards; differences in development between countries

objectives.text: Explain the reasons for differences in living standards and income distribution within and between countries.
Explain how differences in income, productivity, population growth, sectors, saving and investment, education, healthcare and natural resources cause differences in development.
Distinguish absolute from relative poverty.
Explain the causes of poverty.
Explain policies to alleviate poverty and redistribute income.
Define birth rate, death rate and net migration and explain why they vary between countries.

children.name: Effects of changes in the size and structure of populations

objectives.text: Explain the concept of an optimum population and the effects of changes in the size and in the age and gender structure of a population.
Define specialisation by country, explain its basis in the best resource allocation or lowest cost, and its advantages and disadvantages.
Define free trade and explain its advantages and disadvantages.
Define globalisation.
Explain the causes of changes in globalisation and their effects on trade, competition, the environment, migration, income distribution and development.
Explain the advantages and disadvantages of MNCs to host and home countries.
Describe tariffs, import quotas, subsidies and embargoes.
Explain the reasons for trade restrictions.
Explain the consequences of trade restrictions for the home country and its partners, and the advantages and disadvantages of restricting trade.
Define the foreign exchange rate.
Explain the reasons for buying and selling foreign currencies.
Explain how a floating exchange rate is determined, define appreciation and depreciation, and explain the causes of fluctuations.
Explain how exchange rate changes affect the prices of and demand for exports and imports.

children.name: Current account of the balance of payments

objectives.text: Describe the components of the current account and calculate deficits and surpluses on it and its sections.

children.name: Causes, consequences and policies for current account imbalances

objectives.text: Explain the reasons for current account deficits and surpluses.
Explain the impact of deficits and surpluses on GDP, employment, inflation and the exchange rate.
Evaluate the policies available to achieve balance of payments stability.
